title: Chapter 35 — The Mast-Head
paragraphs: It was during the more pleasant weather that my first turn at the masthead came around, in due rotation with the other seamen.

On most American whalers, the mastheads are manned almost as soon as the ship leaves port, even though she may have fifteen thousand miles or more to sail before reaching her proper cruising ground. And if, after a three, four, or five-year voyage, she's heading home with anything unfilled — even an empty vial — then her mastheads stay manned to the last. Not until her skysail-poles, the very tops of her masts, sail in among the spires of the port does she give up the hope of catching one more whale.

Now, since the business of standing mastheads, ashore or afloat, is a very ancient and interesting one, let us enlarge on it here to some extent. I take it that the earliest masthead-standers were the old Egyptians, because in all my research I find none before them. For though their forebears, the builders of Babel, must doubtless have meant their tower to be the loftiest masthead in all Asia, or Africa either, yet since (before the final truck, the wooden cap at the very top of a mast, was put to it) that great stone mast of theirs may be said to have gone by the board in the dread gale of God's wrath, we cannot give these Babel builders priority over the Egyptians. And that the Egyptians were a nation of masthead-standers is an assertion based on the general belief among archaeologists that the first pyramids were founded for astronomical purposes — a theory singularly supported by the peculiar stair-like formation of all four sides of those buildings, by which, with prodigiously long liftings of their legs, those old astronomers used to climb to the apex and sing out for new stars, just as the lookouts of a modern ship sing out for a sail, or a whale just coming into sight. In Saint Stylites, the famous Christian hermit of old times, who built himself a lofty stone pillar in the desert and spent the whole latter part of his life on its summit, hoisting his food up from the ground with a tackle — in him we have a remarkable instance of a dauntless masthead-stander, who was not to be driven from his place by fogs or frosts, rain, hail, or sleet, but, valiantly facing everything out to the last, literally died at his post. Of modern masthead-standers we have only a lifeless set: mere stone, iron, and bronze men, who, though well able to face out a stiff gale, are still entirely incompetent at the business of singing out on discovering any strange sight. There is Napoleon, who stands with arms folded on top of the column of Vendome, some one hundred and fifty feet in the air, careless now who rules the decks below, whether Louis Philippe, Louis Blanc, or Louis the Devil. Great Washington, too, stands high aloft on his towering main-mast in Baltimore, and like one of Hercules' pillars, his column marks that point of human grandeur beyond which few mortals will go. Admiral Nelson, also, stands his masthead on a capstan of gun-metal in Trafalgar Square; and even when he is most obscured by that London smoke, there is still a token that a hidden hero is there; for where there is smoke, there must be fire. But neither great Washington, nor Napoleon, nor Nelson will answer a single hail from below, however madly they are invoked to help with their counsel the distracted decks they gaze down on — however it may be surmised that their spirits penetrate the thick haze of the future and see what shoals and what rocks must be avoided.

It may seem unjustified to link the masthead-standers of the land with those of the sea in any way, but that in truth it is not is plainly shown by a detail for which Obed Macy, the sole historian of Nantucket, is our source. Worthy Obed tells us that in the early days of the whale fishery, before ships were regularly sent out in pursuit, the islanders erected tall poles along the coast, to which lookouts climbed by means of nailed rungs, like chickens going up stairs in a henhouse. A few years ago, the same system was adopted by the bay whalemen of New Zealand, who, upon spotting whales, signaled the waiting boats near the beach. But this custom is now obsolete. So let us turn to the proper masthead: that of a whale ship at sea. The three mastheads are manned from sunrise to sunset, the sailors taking regular turns (as at the helm) and relieving each other every two hours. In the calm weather of the tropics, the masthead is exceedingly pleasant; no, to a dreamy, meditative man it is delightful. There you stand, a hundred feet above the silent decks, striding across the deep as if the masts were giant stilts. Beneath you and between your legs, so to speak, swim the largest monsters of the sea, just as ships once sailed between the boots of the famous Colossus of Rhodes. There you stand, lost in the infinite series of the sea, with nothing stirred but the waves. The hypnotized ship lazily rolls. The drowsy trade winds blow. Everything dissolves you into lethargy. For the most part, in this tropical whaling life, a sublime uneventfulness wraps around you. You hear no news. You read no newspapers. No extras with alarming reports of ordinary events trick you into unnecessary excitement. You hear of no family troubles or bankrupt investments or falling stocks. You never worry about what to have for dinner — all your meals for three years or more are snugly stowed in casks, and your menu is fixed.

On one of those southern whalers, on a long voyage of three or four years, as often happens, the hours you spend at the masthead add up to several whole months. And it's a great pity that the place where you spend so large a share of your entire natural life should be so sadly lacking in anything like cozy homeliness, or anything suited to breeding a comfortable sense of belonging to a spot, such as goes with a bed, a hammock, a hearse, a sentry box, a pulpit, a coach, or any of those other small, snug contraptions in which men shut themselves away for a time. Your usual perch is the top of the topgallant mast, where you stand on two thin parallel sticks (almost unique to whalemen) called the topgallant crosstrees. Up there, tossed about by the sea, the beginner feels roughly as cozy as he would standing on a bull's horns. Of course, in cold weather you can take your house aloft with you in the form of a watch-coat; but strictly speaking, the thickest watch-coat is no more a house than your bare body is. For just as the soul is glued inside its fleshly tabernacle, and can't move around freely in it, or even move out of it, without great risk of perishing (like an ignorant pilgrim crossing the snowy Alps in winter), so a watch-coat is not so much a house as a mere envelope, or an extra skin wrapped around you. You can't put a shelf or a chest of drawers inside your body, and neither can you make a handy closet out of your watch-coat.

On all this, it is much to be regretted that the mastheads of a southern whale ship are not provided with those enviable little tents or pulpits called crow's-nests, in which the lookouts of a Greenland whaler are protected from the inclement weather of the frozen seas. In the fireside narrative of Captain Sleet, titled "A Voyage among the Icebergs, in quest of the Greenland Whale, and incidentally for the re-discovery of the Lost Icelandic Colonies of Old Greenland" — in this admirable volume, all masthead-standers are furnished with a charmingly circumstantial account of the then recently invented crow's-nest of the Glacier, which was the name of Captain Sleet's good ship. He called it the Sleet's crow's-nest, in honor of himself, since he was the original inventor and patentee, and free from all ridiculous false delicacy; and he held that if we name our own children after ourselves (we fathers being the original inventors and patentees), we should likewise name after ourselves any other apparatus we may beget. In shape, the Sleet's crow's-nest is something like a large tierce or pipe (both big casks); it is open above, however, where it is fitted with a movable side-screen to keep to windward of your head in a hard gale. Since it is fixed on the top of the mast, you climb into it through a little trap-hatch in the bottom. On the after side, the side nearest the stern of the ship, is a comfortable seat, with a locker underneath for umbrellas, comforters, and coats. In front is a leather rack in which to keep your speaking trumpet, pipe, telescope, and other nautical conveniences. When Captain Sleet in person stood his masthead in this crow's-nest of his, he tells us that he always had a rifle with him (also fixed in the rack), together with a powder flask and shot, for the purpose of popping off the stray narwhales, or vagrant sea unicorns, infesting those waters; for you cannot shoot at them successfully from the deck, owing to the resistance of the water, but to shoot down on them is a very different thing. Now, it was plainly a labor of love for Captain Sleet to describe, as he does, all the little detailed conveniences of his crow's-nest. But though he enlarges on many of these, and though he treats us to a very scientific account of his experiments in this crow's-nest with a small compass he kept there to counteract the errors resulting from what is called the "local attraction" of all binnacle magnets — an error attributable to the horizontal nearness of the iron in the ship's planks, and, in the Glacier's case, perhaps to there having been so many broken-down blacksmiths among her crew — I say, though the Captain is very discreet and scientific here, yet for all his learned "binnacle deviations," "azimuth compass observations," and "approximate errors," he knows very well, Captain Sleet, that he was not so immersed in those profound magnetic meditations as not to be attracted now and then toward that well-replenished little case-bottle so nicely tucked in on one side of his crow's-nest, within easy reach of his hand. Though, on the whole, I greatly admire and even love the brave, the honest, and learned Captain, yet I take it very ill of him that he should so utterly ignore that case-bottle, seeing what a faithful friend and comforter it must have been while, with mittened fingers and hooded head, he was studying the mathematics up there in that bird's nest within three or four perches of the pole.

But if we southern whale-fishers aren't as snugly housed aloft as Captain Sleet and his Greenlandmen were, that disadvantage is greatly offset by the sharply contrasting serenity of those seductive seas where we mostly sail. For one, I used to lounge up the rigging quite leisurely, resting in the top for a chat with Queequeg or anyone else off duty I might find there. Then I'd climb a little higher, throw a lazy leg over the topsail yard, take a preliminary survey of the watery pastures, and at last reach my final destination.

Let me make a clean confession here and frankly admit that I kept a poor watch. With the problem of the universe revolving in my head, how could I — left completely alone at such a thought-provoking altitude — how could I take seriously my duty to observe all whale-ship standing orders: "Keep your weather eye open and sing out every time."

And let me here movingly warn you ship-owners of Nantucket! Beware of enlisting in your vigilant fisheries any lad with a lean brow and hollow eye, given to unseasonable meditation, who offers to ship with the Phaedon (Plato's dialogue on the immortality of the soul) instead of Bowditch (the standard navigation manual) in his head. Beware of such a one, I say: your whales must be seen before they can be killed, and this sunken-eyed young Platonist will tow you ten wakes around the world and never make you one pint of sperm the richer. Nor are these warnings at all unneeded. For nowadays the whale fishery provides an asylum for many romantic, melancholy, and absent-minded young men, disgusted with the gnawing cares of earth, and seeking sentiment in tar and blubber. Childe Harold not infrequently perches himself on the masthead of some luckless, disappointed whale ship, and in moody phrases exclaims:
"Roll on, thou deep and dark blue ocean, roll! Ten thousand blubber-hunters sweep over thee in vain."

Very often the captains of such ships scold these absent-minded young philosophers, criticizing them for not taking enough "interest" in the voyage — half-hinting that they are so hopelessly lost to all honorable ambition that they would secretly rather not see whales at all. But it's useless. These young Platonists have a theory that their vision is imperfect. They are nearsighted. What use, then, to strain their eyes? They've left their opera glasses at home.

"Why, you monkey," said a harpooner to one of these lads, "we've been cruising now hard on three years, and you haven't spotted a whale yet. Whales are as scarce as hen's teeth whenever you're up here." Perhaps they were. Or perhaps there might have been whole schools of them on the far horizon. But lulled into such an opium-like daze of vacant, unconscious daydreaming is this absent-minded youth — by the blending rhythm of waves and thoughts — that at last he loses his identity. He takes the mystic ocean at his feet for the visible image of that deep, blue, bottomless soul pervading all mankind and nature. Every strange, half-glimpsed, gliding, beautiful thing that escapes him, every dimly perceived rising fin of some unidentifiable form, seems to him the embodiment of those elusive thoughts that populate the soul by continually flitting through it. In this enchanted state, your spirit ebbs away to where it came from, becoming diffused through time and space, like Cranmer's sprinkled Pantheistic ashes, forming at last a part of every shore the round globe over.

There is no life in you now, except the rocking life given by a gently rolling ship — borrowed from the sea, and by the sea from the unfathomable tides of God. But while this sleep, this dream is upon you, move your foot or hand an inch — slip your grip even slightly — and your identity comes rushing back in horror. Over Descartian vortices you hover. And perhaps, at midday, in the fairest weather, with one half-strangled shriek you drop through that transparent air into the summer sea, never to rise again. Take heed, you Pantheists!
